$$

$$

What is the missing expression?
questions.worked_solution:
The boundary of a set $A,$ denoted $∂A,$ is the set that contains all the boundary points of $A.$

The set $A$ and its boundary $∂A$ are shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14134863/assets/0fc95ee69ce7121c0cf8ae68029b135d9667f50275227d141f1d979f85408859.png)

From the diagram, the boundary points of $A$ lie on the  parabola $-2y={x}^{2}.$ 

Therefore,  

$$
∂A=\{(x,y)\in {R}^{2}\,:\,-2y={x}^{2}\,\}.
$$

The interior of $A$ is given by

$$
\text{int}\,A=\{(x,y)\in {R}^{2}\,:\,\bbox[5px,border: 1px solid black]{\phantom{AAAAA}},\,0<y<2\}.
$$

questions.worked_solution:

The interior of a set $A,$ denoted $\text{int}\,A,$ is the set containing all the interior points of $A.$ It contains every point in $A$ except the boundary points: 

$$
\text{int}\,A=A-∂A
$$

The interior of $A$ is shown below.

questions.problem:
Consider the set $A,$ defined by 

$$
A=\{(x,y)\in {R}^{2}\,:\,y\ge 2-x\}.
$$

Which of the following statements are true?

I. $A$ contains none of its boundary points.

II. $A$ contains some (not all) of its boundary points.

III. $\text{int}\,A\ne A$
questions.worked_solution:
The boundary of a set $A,$ denoted $∂A,$ is the set that contains all the boundary points of $A.$

In this case, the set $A$ and its boundary $∂A$ are shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14134863/assets/cdca164d343d8bff4c78a1e366e52c588ca6c54dfdea61acea1900bcbdc79f31.png)

The interior of a set $A,$ denoted $\text{int}\,A,$ is the set containing all the interior points of $A.$ It contains every point in $A$ except the boundary points: 

$$
\text{int}\,A=A-∂A
$$

Notice that, in this case, the set $A$ contains all of its boundary points.

With that in mind, let's examine each statement:

- Statements I and II are false. As we have seen, $A$ contains all its boundary points.

- Statement III is true. Since $A$ contains all of its boundary points, we must have $A-∂A⊊A.$ Therefore $\text{int}\,A\ne A.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "III only."

What is the missing expression?

III. $A = \textrm{int}\,A \cup \partial A$

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
The **boundary** of a set $S,$ denoted $\partial S,$ is the set that contains all the boundary points of $S.$

For example, consider the set $A,$ given by 

$$
A = \big\{ (x,y)\in\mathbb R^2 \,:\, -1 \lt x \leq 1, \, 0 \lt y \leq 2 \big\}.
$$

We can represent this set as the following shaded region.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14134863/assets/5033928a09f9c320973a223bfd49b4b67924b433c7ba53e58bc07a95905f4231.png)

Then, the set $\partial A,$ the boundary of $A,$ has the following representation in the plane.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14134863/assets/e2034b17b6a6834c1d747e2eba4a2522c43e9ff888d5f7feb7bf716b3e2cec00.png)

The **interior** of a set $S,$ denoted $\textrm{int}\, S,$ is the set containing all the interior points of $S.$ It contains every point in $S$ except the boundary points: 

$$
\textrm{int}\,S = S - \partial S
$$

For our set $A$ defined above, the interior looks as follows:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14134863/assets/57ab8735d761926a36aa0e469b4637482c31880cc446d913f93755a12ec65a8f.png)

More formally, the interior of $A$ is given by

$$
\textrm{int}\,A = \big\{ (x,y)\in\mathbb R^2 \,:\, -1 \lt x \lt 1, \, 0 \lt y \lt 2 \big\}.
$$
